head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: How many positions have each absolute difference
Each operation changes a difference by 1 (moving either `nums1[i]` or `nums2[i]` by 1), so only the multiset of differences matters
Number of positions currently at the top level `v`
Operations needed to bring the whole group down to the next distinct value
Spread the remaining `k` evenly over the group: `q` full steps for everyone, `r` of them get one more
Squared cost of the flattened group, plus the untouched smaller differences

p: `nums1 = [1,2,3,4]`, `nums2 = [2,10,20,19]`, `k1 = 4`, `k2 = 3`. Differences are 1, 8, 17, 15. With `k = 0` the cost is 1 + 64 + 289 + 225 = 579. With 7 operations:

blocks.p: With 7 operations the minimal sum of squared differences is 378: the budget flattens the biggest differences (17 and 15) down toward the next level, and the remaining operations are spread evenly over the group.

blocks.h: Why reduce the largest differences first?
p: The cost is the sum of squares, which is convex: reducing a large value saves more than reducing a small one (a drop from 17 to 16 saves 33, from 2 to 1 saves 3). So always lowering the current maximum is optimal, and doing it level by level on the whole group is the fast way to simulate that.

head: Approach
Time
rows: use a max-heap, decrement one at a time
flatten level by level on sorted distinct values (this code)

2333.takeaway: Minimum sum of squared differences: only absolute differences matter; spend the combined budget lowering the largest differences level by level, spreading the remainder evenly.

2336.takeaway: Smallest infinite set: a counter for the untouched tail plus a min-heap (and a set) for numbers added back.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: The LARGEST number seen so far with digit sum `s`
For a fixed digit sum, only the biggest earlier number can give the best pair
The best pair sum ending with this number
Pair with the previous maximum of the same class
Update the maximum for the class AFTER using it
So a number doesn't pair with itself

blocks.h: Why only keep the maximum per digit sum?
p: A pair needs two numbers with the same digit sum. For the new number `x`, the best partner is the largest earlier number in its class, so storing just that maximum (not every number) is enough and the whole thing is one pass.

bullets: Time: O(n · d) for d digits.
Space: O(number of distinct digit sums) ≤ 82.

2342.takeaway: Max pair with equal digit sums: group by digit sum and keep the largest number per group while scanning.

p: A mountain is hidden if its base lies inside another's base. blocks.h: Why is this the right definition of 'first'?
p: The question is about the letter that appears twice FIRST, i.e. whose second occurrence has the smallest index. head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The last element never needs to change; each element only has to be ≤ the element to its right
The smallest value the next element must not exceed
Already fine: it becomes the new bound
Minimum number of parts to split `x` so that each part is ≤ `prev`
Splitting into `k` parts takes `k − 1` replacement operations
Make the parts as equal as possible; the SMALLEST part is `x // k` and becomes the new bound for the element on the left
Maximise the smallest part to give the left element the most room

blocks.h: Why make the parts as equal as possible?
p: Splitting `9` into `3 + 3 + 3` gives a smallest part of 3, which is the largest possible minimum for 3 parts. A larger minimum part means the element to the left may be larger without needing more splits. Uneven parts like `1 + 4 + 4` would have a smaller minimum and force more work to the left.

2366.takeaway: Minimum replacements to sort: scan from the right; split each too-large element into the fewest parts ≤ the bound, with equal parts to maximise the new bound.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Push the next unused digit (digits 1, 2, 3, … in order, each used once)
Using digits in increasing order is what makes the result smallest
On an increase (or at the end) the pending digits can be emitted
Pop in REVERSE order: a run of `D`s means the digits in the run must decrease, so reverse them
Reversing a block turns an increasing sequence into a decreasing one

p: `pattern = "IIIDIDDD"`:

blocks.h: Why does reversing blocks give the smallest number?
p: Each maximal run of `D`s needs a decreasing run of digits. The smallest way to satisfy it is to take the next consecutive unused digits and reverse them. Each `I` then starts with the next, larger unused digits, so earlier positions stay as small as possible.

2375.takeaway: Smallest number from a DI string: push digits 1..n+1 on a stack and flush (reversed) whenever you reach an 'I' or the end.
